Plant: Castor (Ricinus communis) | Section: Identification and description
Castor (Ricinus communis), family Euphorbiaceae.
Also known as: Castor-oil plant, Erand, Eranda.
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Oleum Ricini (castor oil, fixed oil from the seeds of Ricinus communis L.), pp. 271-272; GBIF Backbone Taxonomy: Ricinus communis L. (ACCEPTED, family Euphorbiaceae); DIMPSAR: Dataset for Indian medicinal plant species analysis and recognition (Table 2, 80 species), Table 2, row 12

Plant: Castor (Ricinus communis) | Section: Identification and description
The castor-oil plant (Ricinus communis L.) varies from an annual, monoecious herb in temperate regions to a tree up to 15 m high in some tropical areas, and there are hundreds of forms that differ in size, stem and leaf colour, branching, and seed size and markings. Shoots and flower clusters are glaucous. Leaves are large, alternate, long-stalked, peltate and palmate with 5-12 lobes; the lobes are toothed (serrate or dentate) and the leaves are green or reddish. The flowers are borne in a raceme 30-60 cm high, with female flowers above male ones. The fruit is a 3-celled capsule, usually covered with soft spines, that splits into 3 parts, each holding an oval, mottled seed. WHO describes the seeds as poisonous. The WHO monograph covers only the fixed oil pressed from the seeds. The sources reviewed do not assess the leaf, which is the part the image classifier photographs, so nothing here establishes the leaf as poisonous or as safe.
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Oleum Ricini (castor oil, fixed oil from the seeds of Ricinus communis L.), pp. 271-272; GBIF Backbone Taxonomy: Ricinus communis L. (ACCEPTED, family Euphorbiaceae); DIMPSAR: Dataset for Indian medicinal plant species analysis and recognition (Table 2, 80 species), Table 2, row 12

Plant: Castor (Ricinus communis) | Section: Identification and description
Native range: Indigenous to tropical regions of Africa, probably native to Ethiopia; now adapted and cultivated in subtropical to temperate areas.
Habitat: Cultivated, or growing wild, in most tropical and warm temperate countries.
Image-classifier label for this plant: Castor.
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Oleum Ricini (castor oil, fixed oil from the seeds of Ricinus communis L.), pp. 271-272; GBIF Backbone Taxonomy: Ricinus communis L. (ACCEPTED, family Euphorbiaceae); DIMPSAR: Dataset for Indian medicinal plant species analysis and recognition (Table 2, 80 species), Table 2, row 12

Plant: Castor (Ricinus communis) | Section: Traditional use
The WHO monograph on castor oil lists these uses described in traditional medicine: as an emmenagogue, to induce labour, and for burns, bronchitis, diarrhoea, itching, earache, haemorrhoids, pneumonia, rheumatism and sprains. These refer to the oil. Traditional use reflects cultural and historical practice and does not by itself establish efficacy or safety, and several of these uses carry the safety limits given in the safety section.
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Oleum Ricini (castor oil, fixed oil from the seeds of Ricinus communis L.), p. 274

Plant: Castor (Ricinus communis) | Section: Phytochemistry
Ricinoleic acid (as the triglyceride ricinolein) (Hydroxylated unsaturated C18 fatty acid): Main constituent of castor oil (85-92% of its fatty acids; ricinolein 70-77% of the oil). WHO describes ricinoleate as the local irritant in the small intestine responsible for the oil's laxative effect. WHO describes the mechanism as follows: ricinoleic acid released in the small intestine increases fluid and electrolyte secretion and stimulates peristalsis, with evacuation taking place within 1-6 hours. [evidence: Limited Clinical Evidence]
Palmitic, stearic, oleic, linoleic, linolenic and eicosenoic acids (Other fatty acids of the oil): Minor fatty acids of castor oil (each at most a few per cent). No separate activity is attributed to them in the monograph. [evidence: Insufficient Evidence]
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Oleum Ricini (castor oil, fixed oil from the seeds of Ricinus communis L.), pp. 273-274, 277

Plant: Castor (Ricinus communis) | Section: Evidence for medicinal use
WHO's monograph (Volume 4, 2009) covers castor oil only: the fixed oil obtained by cold expression from the seeds. It lists no uses supported by clinical data. Pharmacopoeial uses are short-term laxative use and external use. Evidence for labour induction is insufficient. No source reviewed supports a medicinal use of castor leaves or raw castor seeds. WHO identifies the seeds as poisonous; the sources reviewed do not assess the leaf, which is the part the plant-identification model sees.
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Oleum Ricini (castor oil, fixed oil from the seeds of Ricinus communis L.), pp. 274-278

Plant: Castor (Ricinus communis) | Section: Evidence for medicinal use
Short-term constipation and bowel evacuation before surgery (castor oil, taken by mouth) (evidence level: Traditional Use Supported). WHO lists castor oil (the fixed oil pressed from the seeds) among uses described in pharmacopoeias and well-established documents: short-term treatment (3-5 days) of acute constipation when dietary measures or bulk-forming laxatives have not given adequate relief, and use as a cathartic for bowel evacuation before surgery.
Topical dermatoses and dermatitis (castor oil, external use) (evidence level: Traditional Use Supported). WHO lists external use of castor oil for topical dermatoses and dermatitis among uses described in pharmacopoeias and well-established documents. WHO also records that castor oil can itself cause contact dermatitis and cheilitis (inflammation of the lips) in some people.
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Oleum Ricini (castor oil, fixed oil from the seeds of Ricinus communis L.), pp. 274-278

Plant: Castor (Ricinus communis) | Section: Evidence for medicinal use
Induction of labour (castor oil, taken by mouth) (evidence level: Insufficient Evidence). Castor oil has been widely used traditionally to start labour, but the evidence is insufficient. A Cochrane review of three trials (233 women, single doses of castor oil) reported small numbers, poor methodological quality and no data on maternal or neonatal harm, and all women who took the oil felt nauseous. WHO concludes there is insufficient evidence to support the safety and efficacy of the oil for this purpose. WHO lists the oil as contraindicated as a laxative in pregnancy before 40 weeks, and use after 40 weeks needs the supervision of a physician, midwife or other experienced professional.
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Oleum Ricini (castor oil, fixed oil from the seeds of Ricinus communis L.), pp. 274-278; Kelly AJ et al. 2013, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013(7):CD003099 (PMID 23881775)

Plant: Castor (Ricinus communis) | Section: Preparation and dosage
Cold-pressed castor oil (pharmaceutical fixed oil): WHO defines the material as the fixed oil obtained by cold expression from the seeds. Dosage forms listed are the fixed oil and capsules; it is to be kept in well-closed containers protected from light. The WHO monograph gives no home preparation from leaves, seeds or other plant parts, and the raw seeds are poisonous. Plant part: Seed (pressed to give the fixed oil). Intended use: Short-term oral laxative; external use on the skin. Safety note: Raw castor seeds are poisonous; see the safety section.
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Oleum Ricini (castor oil, fixed oil from the seeds of Ricinus communis L.), pp. 272, 281

Plant: Castor (Ricinus communis) | Section: Preparation and dosage
Dose, Castor oil (fixed oil) (Oral, General (contraindicated in children under 12 years, in pregnancy before 40 weeks and while breastfeeding)): 1-10 ml; Single daily dose; maximum duration: 3-5 days; do not take for more than 3-5 days without consulting a health care professional. Source: WHO monograph posology (Volume 4, p. 281), laxative use. A WHO-listed dose range for labour induction under medical supervision is deliberately not reproduced here, because WHO states the evidence for that use is insufficient and requires professional supervision. Flagged for human review.
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Oleum Ricini (castor oil, fixed oil from the seeds of Ricinus communis L.), pp. 272, 281

Plant: Castor (Ricinus communis) | Section: Safety and precautions
Contraindication - Castor seeds (castor beans), if eaten or chewed: SAFETY NOTICE: castor seeds are poisonous. WHO describes the seeds of Ricinus communis as poisonous, and poisoning after eating castor beans is documented. Ricin, a protein toxin from the castor bean plant, is the toxin in these poisonings. Symptoms can start within about 12 hours and may include nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and abdominal pain, and in severe cases hypotension, liver failure, kidney dysfunction and death from multi-organ failure. A JAMA review states there is no antidote, vaccine or other specific therapy, and that prompt supportive care is needed. Absorption after swallowing is erratic and toxin is released when seeds are chewed. This is a poisoning hazard of the seeds (beans), not a medicinal use.
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Oleum Ricini (castor oil, fixed oil from the seeds of Ricinus communis L.), pp. 279-281; Audi J et al. 2005, JAMA 294(18):2342-2351 (PMID 16278363); Lopez Nunez OF et al. 2017, J Emerg Med 53(5):e67-e71 (PMID 28987302)

Plant: Castor (Ricinus communis) | Section: Safety and precautions
Advisory - Castor leaf photographs: what the seed notice does and does not say: The seed hazard above is documented for the seeds (beans). The sources reviewed do not assess the castor leaf, so they establish the leaf neither as poisonous nor as safe. A leaf photo identified as castor is not a statement about seed toxicity or leaf toxicity. The seed hazard is also separate from castor oil, which WHO describes as the fixed oil obtained by cold expression from the seeds.
Contraindication - Pregnant women: WHO states castor oil should not be used as a laxative during pregnancy, and that it is contraindicated as a laxative in pregnancy before 40 weeks because of potential induction of labour. Use for labour induction after 40 weeks requires the supervision of a physician, midwife or other experienced professional.
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Oleum Ricini (castor oil, fixed oil from the seeds of Ricinus communis L.), pp. 279-281; Kelly AJ et al. 2013, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013(7):CD003099 (PMID 23881775)

Plant: Castor (Ricinus communis) | Section: Safety and precautions
Contraindication - Nursing mothers: WHO lists castor oil as contraindicated in breastfeeding mothers: ricinoleic acid is absorbed into the bloodstream and excreted into human breast milk, and in suckling infants it has a purgative effect.
Contraindication - Children under 12 years: WHO states castor oil should not be used as a laxative in children under 12 years.
Contraindication - People with biliary, intestinal or abdominal conditions, or dehydration: WHO states the oil should not be used by people with biliary tract obstruction or other biliary disorders (it stimulates bile flow), appendicitis, chronic inflammatory bowel disorders, undiagnosed abdominal pain, severe dehydration with loss of salt and water, or intestinal blockage and ileus.
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Oleum Ricini (castor oil, fixed oil from the seeds of Ricinus communis L.), pp. 279-281

Plant: Castor (Ricinus communis) | Section: Safety and precautions
Contraindication - People with hypersensitivity or allergy to castor oil or castor beans: WHO lists hypersensitivity or allergy to the oil as a contraindication. It also records allergy to castor beans, asthma in oil-industry workers, seamen and laboratory workers exposed to the beans, occupational dermatitis from handling the plant or beans, and rare allergic contact dermatitis from cosmetics containing the oil. A rash (exanthema) means the oil should be stopped and not used again.
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Oleum Ricini (castor oil, fixed oil from the seeds of Ricinus communis L.), pp. 279-281

Plant: Castor (Ricinus communis) | Section: Safety and precautions
Monitoring Required - General (all users of the oil as a laxative): Cathartics taken for more than a few days may worsen intestinal hypomotility; WHO advises not to take castor oil for more than 3-5 days without consulting a health care professional. Higher doses can cause stomach upset, nausea, vomiting, painful abdominal cramps and severe diarrhoea with loss of water and electrolytes; continued use or misuse can require intravenous rehydration, and excessive potassium loss may disturb heart function and cause muscle weakness. Reduce the dose or stop, and consult a health care professional, if these occur.
Drug interaction - Cardiac glycosides (for example digoxin) (severity: Not graded in source): WHO states that using castor oil together with cardiac glycosides may increase the risk of adverse events because of fluid and electrolyte losses.
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Oleum Ricini (castor oil, fixed oil from the seeds of Ricinus communis L.), pp. 279-281

Plant: Castor (Ricinus communis) | Section: Safety and precautions
Drug interaction - Antiarrhythmic drugs, diuretics, cortisol (corticosteroids), liquorice, antihistamines and fat-soluble vitamins (severity: Not graded in source): WHO states that using castor oil together with these may reduce their efficacy.
Overdose: Overdose can cause nausea, vomiting, painful abdominal cramps and severe diarrhoea with loss of water and electrolytes; consult a health care professional about replacing fluid and electrolytes. Excessive potassium loss can disturb heart function and cause muscle weakness (WHO). Eating castor seeds is a separate and more serious poisoning hazard (see the safety warnings).
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Oleum Ricini (castor oil, fixed oil from the seeds of Ricinus communis L.), pp. 279-281

Plant: Guava (Psidium guajava) | Section: Identification and description
Guava (Psidium guajava), family Myrtaceae.
Also known as: Amrud, Amrood, Guayaba, Goiaba, Guava tree.
Guava (Psidium guajava L.) is a large shrub or small tree up to 10 m high. The bark is brownish, thin and smooth, often flaking off in scaly patches. Leaves are opposite, oblong to slightly oval, 5-15 cm long, light green on the upper surface and downy and pale green on the underside, with prominent veins on the underside; the margin is smooth or dentate and the venation reticulate. Flowers are white, about 2.5 cm across, single or a few together in the leaf axils, with numerous stamens. Fruits are globose or pear-shaped, usually yellow, 2.5-10 cm long, and contain many seeds. The WHO monograph covers the dried and/or young leaves.
Native range: Native to tropical America; now pantropical.
Image-classifier label for this plant: Guava.
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Folium Guavae (guava leaf, Psidium guajava L.), pp. 127-128; GBIF Backbone Taxonomy: Psidium guajava L. (ACCEPTED, family Myrtaceae); DIMPSAR: Dataset for Indian medicinal plant species analysis and recognition (Table 2, 80 species), Table 2, row 20

Plant: Guava (Psidium guajava) | Section: Traditional use
The WHO monograph lists these uses described in traditional medicine: abdominal pain, bleeding gums, cough, gastritis, headache, ringworm, vaginitis, wounds and worms; also as an astringent, an antiemetic and an emmenagogue. Traditional use reflects cultural and historical practice and does not by itself establish efficacy. The WHO monograph found no uses described in pharmacopoeias or other well-established documents.
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Folium Guavae (guava leaf, Psidium guajava L.), p. 130

Plant: Guava (Psidium guajava) | Section: Phytochemistry
Quercetin and quercetin glycosides (including guajaverin) (Flavonol): WHO identifies quercetin as the main active constituent of a leaf extract that inhibited the peristaltic reflex of isolated guinea-pig ileum (laboratory finding). [evidence: Preclinical Evidence Only]
Ellagic acid, guavins A, C and D, gallocatechin (Tannins and related polyphenols): Listed as constituents of the leaf. WHO reports at least 14% (w/w) tannins as a quality specification. No specific activity is attributed to these compounds in the monograph. [evidence: Insufficient Evidence]
Ursolic acid, oleanolic acid and related triterpene acids (Triterpene acids): Listed as constituents of the leaf. No specific activity is attributed to them in the monograph. [evidence: Insufficient Evidence]
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Folium Guavae (guava leaf, Psidium guajava L.), pp. 129-131

Plant: Guava (Psidium guajava) | Section: Phytochemistry
Leaf essential oil (1,8-cineole, pinene, caryophyllene, bisabolene) (Monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes): WHO reports that the leaf essential oil and one of its major constituents, pinene, reduced pain responses in mice (laboratory finding). WHO specifies at least 0.6% (v/w) essential oil. [evidence: Preclinical Evidence Only]
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Folium Guavae (guava leaf, Psidium guajava L.), pp. 129-131

Plant: Guava (Psidium guajava) | Section: Evidence for medicinal use
Guava leaf has a WHO monograph (Volume 4, 2009). It lists oral use for acute diarrhoea, gingivitis and rotaviral enteritis as supported by clinical data, and finds no pharmacopoeial uses. The human trials it summarises are few and small (50 to 122 participants) and two of them are not indexed in PubMed, so they have not been appraised independently here. Other traditional uses rest on traditional practice and, in part, on laboratory studies.
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Folium Guavae (guava leaf, Psidium guajava L.), pp. 130-135

Plant: Guava (Psidium guajava) | Section: Evidence for medicinal use
Acute diarrhoea (oral leaf preparations) (evidence level: Limited Clinical Evidence). WHO lists oral guava-leaf preparations among uses supported by clinical data for acute diarrhoea, but the trials it summarises are small. In a randomized, double-blind trial of adults with acute diarrhoea (50 per group; capsules of a quercetin-standardised leaf extract, 500 mg every 8 hours for 3 days), the extract was associated with a shorter duration of abdominal pain than placebo. In a randomized, double-blind trial of 122 patients, powdered leaf and tetracycline did not differ significantly in stool output, fluid intake or duration of diarrhoea. An aqueous leaf extract also gave results similar to a kaolin or pectin suspension in small groups. These findings do not extend to other conditions or preparations.
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Folium Guavae (guava leaf, Psidium guajava L.), pp. 130-135; Lozoya X et al. 2002, J Ethnopharmacol 83(1-2):19-24 (PMID 12413703)

Plant: Guava (Psidium guajava) | Section: Evidence for medicinal use
Gingivitis (mouthwash made from a leaf decoction) (evidence level: Limited Clinical Evidence). WHO lists a leaf-decoction mouthwash among uses supported by clinical data for gingivitis. It describes one 3-week, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial of 70 people with gingivitis: those who rinsed three times daily with the leaf-decoction mouthwash had less gingival inflammation (19.8%) and fewer sites of severe gingival disease (40.5%) than those using a placebo mouthwash. This is a single small trial.
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Folium Guavae (guava leaf, Psidium guajava L.), pp. 130-135

Plant: Guava (Psidium guajava) | Section: Evidence for medicinal use
Rotaviral enteritis in infants (leaf decoction) (evidence level: Limited Clinical Evidence). WHO lists a leaf decoction among uses supported by clinical data for rotaviral enteritis. One randomized trial of 62 patients reported recovery within 3 days in 87.1% of the guava group versus 58.1% of the control group (p < 0.05), and a shorter time to the end of diarrhoea (25.1 +/- 9.5 hours versus 38.7 +/- 15.2 hours). According to the PubMed abstract, the control group received Gegen Qinlian decoction, an active comparator rather than placebo. This is a single small trial and WHO separately advises against use in children under 12 years because safety data are lacking.
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Folium Guavae (guava leaf, Psidium guajava L.), pp. 130-135; Wei L et al. 2000, Zhongguo Zhong Xi Yi Jie He Za Zhi 20(12):893-895 (PMID 11938857)

Plant: Guava (Psidium guajava) | Section: Evidence for medicinal use
Experimental activities in animals and laboratory studies (evidence level: Preclinical Evidence Only). In animal, isolated-tissue and laboratory experiments summarised by WHO, guava-leaf extracts or leaf essential oil showed antinociceptive, antidiarrhoeal, antispasmodic, antihyperglycaemic, anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial activity, and activity against Plasmodium falciparum in vitro. These findings come from animals, isolated tissues and cultures and do not establish effects in people.
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Folium Guavae (guava leaf, Psidium guajava L.), pp. 130-135

Plant: Guava (Psidium guajava) | Section: Preparation and dosage
Leaf decoction (as used in a clinical trial): WHO lists crude drug, decoctions, extracts and teas as dosage forms. In the gingivitis trial it summarises, a decoction was made from dried leaves (3 kg in 30 litres of water, boiled for 20 minutes) and used as a mouthwash. These are research quantities, not a household recipe. Plant part: Dried leaves. Intended use: Mouthwash in a gingivitis trial. Safety note: WHO advises against use in pregnancy, while breastfeeding, and in children under 12 years because safety data are lacking.
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Folium Guavae (guava leaf, Psidium guajava L.), pp. 134, 136

Plant: Guava (Psidium guajava) | Section: Preparation and dosage
Dose, Aqueous leaf extract (mouthwash) (Topical (oral rinse), General (participants in a gingivitis trial; ages not stated)): 15 ml; Three times daily, rinsing for at least 1 minute per session; maximum duration: 3 weeks in the trial; WHO gives no maximum duration. Source: WHO monograph posology (Volume 4, p. 136). This is the regimen of the gingivitis trial that WHO cites (ref 26, Kraivaphan 1991), which has no PubMed record. It is listed here from the WHO monograph posology; the primary trial report was not retrieved, so no PMID is given.
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Folium Guavae (guava leaf, Psidium guajava L.), pp. 134, 136

Plant: Guava (Psidium guajava) | Section: Preparation and dosage
Dose, Powdered leaf (capsules) (Oral, General (participants in an acute diarrhoea trial; ages not stated)): 500 mg; Three or four times daily (WHO posology); the trial gave 500 mg every 6 hours; maximum duration: 3 days in the trial; WHO gives no maximum duration but says not to exceed the recommended dose or duration. Source: WHO monograph posology (Volume 4, p. 136). The trial WHO cites (ref 50, Thanangkul 1987, which has no PubMed record) gave 500 mg every 6 hours for 3 days; WHO's posology states three or four times daily. It is listed here from the WHO monograph; the primary trial report was not retrieved, so no PMID is given. WHO does not give a separate dose for children, for whom use under 12 years is not recommended.
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Folium Guavae (guava leaf, Psidium guajava L.), pp. 134, 136

Plant: Guava (Psidium guajava) | Section: Safety and precautions
Precaution - Pregnant women: WHO states that, because safety data are lacking, use of the crude drug (guava leaf) during pregnancy is not recommended. No information on teratogenic effects was found.
Precaution - Nursing mothers: WHO states that, because safety data are lacking, use of the crude drug during breastfeeding is not recommended.
Precaution - Children under 12 years: WHO states that, because safety data are lacking, use of the crude drug in children under 12 years is not recommended. One trial in infants with rotaviral enteritis is summarised by WHO, but a single small trial does not establish safety.
Contraindication - People with hypersensitivity or allergy to guava leaf: WHO lists hypersensitivity or allergy to the plant material as a contraindication. WHO cites one report of allergic dermatitis after external application of a tea prepared from the crude drug.
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Folium Guavae (guava leaf, Psidium guajava L.), pp. 133-136; Obi M et al. 2001, Contact Dermatitis 44(2):116-117 (PMID 11205393)

Plant: Guava (Psidium guajava) | Section: Safety and precautions
Advisory - General (all users): WHO advises not to exceed the recommended dose or duration of treatment. WHO reports no drug-interaction information and no information on carcinogenicity, mutagenicity or fertility.
Drug interactions: none were reported in the sources reviewed for this entry.
Overdose: In a 6-month study in rats, an aqueous leaf extract given at 1, 10 and 100 times the usual therapeutic dose for diarrhoea was associated with changes in blood chemistry (including raised liver enzymes, which WHO describes as signs of hepatotoxicity) and with mild fatty change and kidney changes in the tissue examined. This is an animal finding; its relevance to people is not established.
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Folium Guavae (guava leaf, Psidium guajava L.), pp. 133-136

Plant: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) | Section: Identification and description
Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum), family Solanaceae.
Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum L.) is a member of the nightshade family (Solanaceae) and an important crop worldwide; the fruit is a major food source for humans. This entry treats tomato as a food plant. The sources reviewed do not describe the leaf or plant structure, so no identification aid is given here.
Image-classifier label for this plant: Tomato.
Sources: GBIF Backbone Taxonomy: Solanum lycopersicum L. (ACCEPTED, family Solanaceae); Paulsen E et al. 2012, Contact Dermatitis 67(6):321-327 (PMID 22860619); Friedman M et al. 2002, J Agric Food Chem 50(21):5751-5780 (PMID 12358437); DIMPSAR: Dataset for Indian medicinal plant species analysis and recognition (Table 2, 80 species), Table 2, row 70

Plant: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) | Section: Traditional use
No traditional medicinal use of tomato is documented in the sources reviewed for this entry. Tomato is treated here as a food crop.
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Annex 2, cumulative index of monographs in Volumes 1-4 (alphabetical order of plant name), pp. 395-396 (no tomato monograph)

Plant: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) | Section: Phytochemistry
alpha-Tomatine and dehydrotomatine (Steroidal glycoalkaloids): Bitter-tasting defence compounds. alpha-Tomatine is the major steroidal glycoalkaloid of tomato and accumulates in all plant tissues, particularly in the leaves and immature green fruits; it is the main one reported in unripe green tomatoes. Reviews describe a role in defence against pathogens and herbivores and interactions with cholesterol that disrupt cell membranes (laboratory findings). [evidence: Preclinical Evidence Only]
Lycopene (Carotenoid): A carotenoid with high antioxidant capacity that is present in tomato products. Trials of tomato products and lycopene on cardiovascular risk factors give conflicting results (see the evidence section). [evidence: Insufficient Evidence]
Sources: Liu Y et al. 2023, Plants (Basel) 12(18):3289 (PMID 37765452); Piccolo V et al. 2024, Foods 13(2):331 (PMID 38275698); Friedman M et al. 2002, J Agric Food Chem 50(21):5751-5780 (PMID 12358437); Tierney AC et al. 2020, Adv Nutr 11(6):1453-1488 (PMID 32652029)

Plant: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) | Section: Evidence for medicinal use
Tomato is a food crop, and no WHO monograph exists for it (checked in the cumulative index of WHO Volumes 1-4). Systematic reviews of trials on tomato products and lycopene give conflicting results for cardiovascular risk factors, so the evidence is regarded as insufficient. The sources reviewed contain nothing about tomato leaves as a medicine.
Sources: WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Annex 2, cumulative index of monographs in Volumes 1-4 (alphabetical order of plant name), pp. 395-396 (no tomato monograph)

Plant: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) | Section: Evidence for medicinal use
Cardiovascular risk factors (tomato products and lycopene) (evidence level: Insufficient Evidence). Systematic reviews of intervention trials on tomato products and lycopene disagree. A 2017 meta-analysis of 21 trials reported that tomato supplementation was associated with lower LDL-cholesterol (-0.22 mmol/L) and interleukin-6 and better flow-mediated dilation, and that lycopene supplementation was associated with lower systolic blood pressure (-5.66 mmHg). A 2020 review of 43 studies found no significant difference in blood pressure or blood lipids, with conflicting findings across studies. A 2023 meta-analysis of 34 randomized trials found no effect on most cardiovascular risk factors, apart from a lower level of malondialdehyde, a marker of oxidative stress. Doses and forms of tomato and lycopene varied widely between trials. These reviews concern tomato products and lycopene, not tomato leaves, and the overall evidence is regarded as insufficient.
Sources: Cheng HM et al. 2017, Atherosclerosis 257:100-108 (PMID 28129549); Tierney AC et al. 2020, Adv Nutr 11(6):1453-1488 (PMID 32652029); Zamani M et al. 2023, Curr Pharm Des 29(21):1671-1700 (PMID 37496241); WHO monographs on selected medicinal plants, Vol. 4 (2009): Annex 2, cumulative index of monographs in Volumes 1-4 (alphabetical order of plant name), pp. 395-396 (no tomato monograph)

Plant: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) | Section: Safety and precautions
Precaution - People with tomato allergy, grass-pollen allergy or latex allergy: A review describes tomato as one of the most prevalent allergenic vegetables. Food allergy to tomato can cause symptoms in the gut, skin and lungs, and anaphylactic shock. Tomato allergy is linked to grass-pollen and latex allergy. The data on tomato allergens are not yet sufficient.
Precaution - People with skin sensitivity to plants: Contact dermatitis from tomato plants or fruit is reported as uncommon. In a Danish patch-test series of 93 patients, 8 (9%) reacted to extracts of tomato plants. The plant allergens are unknown, and tomato fruit can also cause protein contact dermatitis.
Sources: Wlodarczyk K et al. 2022, Antioxidants (Basel) 11(4):644 (PMID 35453329); Paulsen E et al. 2012, Contact Dermatitis 67(6):321-327 (PMID 22860619)

Plant: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) | Section: Safety and precautions
Advisory - General (anyone considering eating tomato leaves or green fruit): alpha-Tomatine, a bitter steroidal glycoalkaloid, is concentrated in tomato leaves and immature green fruit. The sources reviewed do not give a safe level of intake for leaves or green fruit, and this entry makes no recommendation about eating them.
Advisory - Pregnant women: No pregnancy-specific safety information was found in the sources reviewed for this entry, and no recommendation is made.
Advisory - Infants and children: No safety information specific to infants or children was found in the sources reviewed for this entry, and no recommendation is made.
Drug interactions: none were reported in the sources reviewed for this entry.
Sources: Liu Y et al. 2023, Plants (Basel) 12(18):3289 (PMID 37765452); Piccolo V et al. 2024, Foods 13(2):331 (PMID 38275698)
